blocks.text: Two gears bought from different suppliers, one marked 3 mm and the other 3.5 mm, will not mesh no matter how carefully they are bored and mounted, because the teeth do not have the same spacing. Gear geometry is a system of agreed dimensions, and the module is the number that has to match.

blocks.markdown: A pair of gears transmits motion by teeth that push on one another along a line of action. For a constant speed ratio the teeth must have an involute profile, which is the curve traced by the end of a taut string unwound from a circle called the base circle. Two imaginary rolling cylinders, the **pitch circles**, touch at the pitch point and roll on each other without slip. Almost every dimension of a spur gear is expressed through these circles.

blocks.title: Module and pitch diameter
blocks.text: The module $m$ (in mm) is the pitch diameter divided by the number of teeth $N$: $m=d/N$, so $d=mN$. The circular pitch is $p=\pi m$, the arc length from one tooth to the next on the pitch circle. Two gears can mesh only if they have the same module and the same pressure angle $\phi$ (the angle between the line of action and the common tangent to the pitch circles; $20^\circ$ is standard in modern practice).

blocks.caption: Pitch diameter, centre distance and speed ratio of an external spur pair (n in rev/min)

blocks.markdown: The speed ratio follows from the pitch circles rolling without slip: both have the same surface speed $\omega_1d_1/2=\omega_2d_2/2$, so the speed ratio is the inverse ratio of pitch diameters, which equals the inverse ratio of tooth numbers because the module is shared. An external pair turns in opposite directions.

blocks.title: Geometry of a 20/60 pair
blocks.prompt: A pinion with $N_1=20$ teeth drives a gear with $N_2=60$ teeth. The module is $m=4$ mm and the pinion turns at $n_1=1440$ rev/min. Find both pitch diameters, the centre distance, the speed ratio, the output speed and the circular pitch.

steps.text: Centre distance is half of the sum of the pitch diameters.
Speed ratio and output speed. The pinion is the smaller, faster gear.
Circular pitch, which must be equal on both gears for them to mesh.

blocks.answer: $d_1=80$ mm, $d_2=240$ mm, $C=160$ mm, speed ratio 3:1 (reduction), $n_2=480$ rev/min and $p=12.57$ mm.

blocks.markdown: **Tooth forces.** The force between meshing teeth acts along the line of action, tilted by the pressure angle from the tangent to the pitch circle. Resolve it into a **tangential component** $W_t$ that does the useful work and transmits torque, and a **radial component** $W_r$ that only pushes the gears apart and loads the bearings. Friction between the teeth is neglected. The torque $T$ on the gear and the transmitted power $P$ give the tangential force; $V$ is the pitch-line speed.

blocks.latex: W_t=\frac{2T}{d}=\frac{P}{V},\quad V=\frac{\pi d n}{60},\quad W_r=W_t\tan\phi,\quad W=\frac{W_t}{\cos\phi}
blocks.caption: Tooth forces on a spur gear (T in N m, d in m, n in rev/min, V in m/s, P in W); W is the total (normal) tooth force

blocks.title: Tooth forces on the 4 mm pinion
blocks.prompt: The 20-tooth pinion above ($d_1=80$ mm, 1440 rev/min) transmits $P=15$ kW with a $20^\circ$ pressure angle. Find the torque, $W_t$, $W_r$, the total tooth force and the pitch-line speed.

steps.text: Angular speed, then torque from power.
Tangential force from torque and pitch radius $0.040$ m.
Pitch-line speed, and a check that $W_t=P/V$ gives the same force.

blocks.markdown: **Undercutting.** The involute exists only outside the base circle. If a pinion has too few teeth, the tool that generates the teeth (or the mating rack) cuts away the root of the involute near the base circle, a defect called undercutting that weakens the tooth and shortens the contact. For a pinion meshing with a rack of full-depth teeth (addendum $k\,m$, with $k=1$) the limiting number of teeth is found by requiring that the rack tip just reaches the base circle. For a pinion meshing with a gear of ratio $m_G=N_G/N_P$ the limit is lower, because the gear's tip is lower, as shown by the second expression.

blocks.caption: Shigley relations for full-depth teeth, k = 1; round up to a whole number of teeth

rows: Older standard, weak teeth needing many teeth
Present standard; 13 teeth is enough for a 1:1 pair
Stronger root, slightly noisier, higher bearing loads
blocks.caption: Minimum teeth to avoid undercutting with a full-depth rack (k = 1)

items: Mesh requirements: equal module $m$ and equal pressure angle $\phi$.
Pitch diameter $d=mN$, centre distance $C=m(N_1+N_2)/2$, speed ratio $N_2/N_1$.
Torque to force: $W_t=2T/d$, then $W_r=W_t\tan\phi$; bearings carry the vector sum.
Avoid undercutting: use at least $N_{min}$ teeth, or a larger pressure angle, or profile-shifted (addendum-modified) teeth.

blocks.title: Units trip up gear problems
blocks.text: Module is in mm but torque equations need metres, and speeds are normally in rev/min but power equations need rad/s. Write the unit beside every number, check that $W_t=P/V$ and $W_t=2T/d$ agree, and remember that the speed ratio uses tooth numbers, not module.

points: Spur gears mesh only with equal module and pressure angle; $d=mN$, $C=m(N_1+N_2)/2$ and the speed ratio is $N_2/N_1$.
Tangential force $W_t=2T/d=P/V$ does the work; radial force $W_r=W_t\tan\phi$ separates the gears and loads the bearings.
Undercutting appears when the pinion has fewer than about $2/\sin^2\phi$ teeth against a rack (17.1 for $20^\circ$), and fewer teeth are allowed when the mate is a gear.
A larger pressure angle permits fewer teeth but increases the radial load on shafts and bearings.

questions.stem: A spur gear has 36 teeth and a pitch diameter of 108 mm. What is its module?

distractorRationale.c: 108 mm is the pitch diameter itself.
distractorRationale.d: 9.42 mm is the circular pitch pi m, not the module.

questions.explanation: The module is defined as pitch diameter divided by tooth number, so $m=108/36=3$ mm. The circular pitch would be $\pi m=9.42$ mm, which is a different quantity.

questions.stem: Which pair of conditions must two external spur gears satisfy in order to mesh correctly?

options.text: The same module and the same pressure angle
The same number of teeth and the same pitch diameter
The same face width and the same bore
The same module and the same speed

questions.correctOptionText: The same module and the same pressure angle

distractorRationale.a: Correct: teeth must have equal spacing and compatible profiles.
distractorRationale.b: Gears with different numbers of teeth mesh perfectly well; that is how speed ratios are achieved.
distractorRationale.c: Face width and bore do not affect conjugate action.
distractorRationale.d: Speeds differ by the gear ratio; they cannot be equal.

questions.explanation: Matching module gives equal circular pitch so the teeth fit the spaces, and matching pressure angle gives compatible involute profiles. Tooth number and bore are free to differ.

questions.stem: Two meshing external spur gears with module 3 mm have 25 and 75 teeth. What is the centre distance?

distractorRationale.b: 300 mm is the sum of the two pitch diameters without halving.
distractorRationale.c: 100 mm uses the number of teeth only in a mistaken way (N1 + N2).
distractorRationale.d: 225 mm is the pitch diameter of the larger gear (3 x 75), not the centre distance.

questions.explanation: The pitch diameters are 75 mm and 225 mm, and the centre distance is half their sum, $C=(75+225)/2=150$ mm. Doubling the number of teeth at the same module doubles the gear sizes and the centre distance.

questions.stem: A $20^\circ$ pressure-angle spur gear pair transmits a tangential tooth force of 3.2 kN. What is the radial force?

distractorRationale.b: 3.41 kN is the total force W_t/cos 20, not the radial component.
distractorRationale.c: 1.09 kN uses sin 20 (3.2 x 0.342) instead of tan 20.
distractorRationale.d: 2.69 kN comes from W_t x tan 40 degrees, which is not a component of the tooth force.

questions.explanation: The line of action is tilted by $\phi$ from the tangent, so $W_r=W_t\tan\phi=3.2\times0.3640=1.165$ kN. The total tooth force is $W_t/\cos\phi=3.41$ kN, which is larger than either component.

questions.stem: Why does a spur pinion with a $14.5^\circ$ pressure angle need more teeth to avoid undercutting than one with a $20^\circ$ pressure angle?

options.text: The base circle is larger for the smaller pressure angle, so the involute starts further out and the tooth root is cut more easily
The $14.5^\circ$ teeth are shorter and so more flexible
The $14.5^\circ$ gear transmits a larger radial force
The $14.5^\circ$ gear has a smaller module

questions.correctOptionText: The base circle is larger for the smaller pressure angle, so the involute starts further out and the tooth root is cut more easily

distractorRationale.a: Correct: base radius is r cos(phi), so a smaller phi puts the base circle closer to the pitch circle, and the usable involute begins nearer the tip.
distractorRationale.b: Tooth stiffness is not what determines undercutting.
distractorRationale.c: Radial force is smaller, not larger, for a small pressure angle.
distractorRationale.d: Module and pressure angle are independent parameters.

questions.explanation: The limit $N_{min}=2k/\sin^2\phi$ rises quickly as $\phi$ falls: 17.1 teeth at $20^\circ$ against 31.9 at $14.5^\circ$. Geometrically the base circle $r_b=r\cos\phi$ is bigger for the smaller angle, so more of the root lies inside it.

questions.stem: A pinion with 18 teeth turns at 1750 rev/min and drives a gear with 72 teeth. Find the speed of the gear in rev/min.
questions.explanation: The speed ratio is $N_2/N_1=72/18=4$, so the gear turns at $1750/4=437.5$ rev/min. The module does not enter, because only tooth numbers fix the speed ratio.

questions.stem: A 24-tooth spur pinion of module 2.5 mm turns at 950 rev/min and transmits 7.5 kW. Find the tangential tooth force in N.
questions.explanation: The pitch diameter is $d=2.5\times24=60$ mm, so the pitch-line speed is $V=\pi\times0.060\times950/60=2.985$ m/s. Then $W_t=P/V=7500/2.985=2513$ N.

questions.stem: A 40-tooth gear of module 5 mm (pressure angle $25^\circ$) receives 240 N m of torque. Find the radial component of the tooth force in N.
questions.explanation: The pitch diameter is $5\times40=200$ mm, so $W_t=2T/d=2\times240/0.200=2400$ N. The radial force is $W_r=W_t\tan25^\circ=2400\times0.4663=1119$ N.

questions.stem: Explain why two spur gears must have the same module and pressure angle to mesh, and show from the no-slip rolling of the pitch circles that the speed ratio is the inverse ratio of tooth numbers.
markingGuide: Teeth must fit into the other gear's spaces, so circular pitch $p=\pi m$ must be equal, which means equal module.
Equal pressure angle (equal base-circle to pitch-circle relation, base pitch $p\cos\phi$) is needed so that the involute profiles are conjugate and the line of action is common.
Pitch circles roll without slip: surface speeds equal, $\omega_1d_1/2=\omega_2d_2/2$.
questions.explanation: The speed ratio is a pure geometric consequence of the pitch-circle contact, and the common module is what lets that ratio be expressed with tooth numbers. Without a common module the pitch-diameter ratio would not equal the tooth-number ratio.

questions.stem: Describe what is meant by undercutting in a spur pinion, state the rack formula for the minimum number of teeth and evaluate it for $\phi=20^\circ$ with full-depth teeth, and list two ways of avoiding undercutting when a small pinion is required.
markingGuide: Undercutting: the generating tool (or rack tip) cuts away the root of the tooth below the base circle, weakening the tooth and removing part of the involute.
Rack formula $N_{min}=2k/\sin^2\phi$ with $k=1$ for full depth.
For $20^\circ$: $\sin^2 20^\circ=0.117$, so $N_{min}=2/0.117=17.1$, so 18 teeth in practice.
Remedy 1: increase the pressure angle (for example $25^\circ$ gives 11.2).
Remedy 2: use a profile-shifted (long-and-short addendum) pinion, or a stub tooth with $k<1$; a pinion running against a gear rather than a rack may have fewer teeth (13 for a 1:1 pair).
questions.explanation: Undercutting is a manufacturing and strength problem, avoided by ensuring that the pinion tooth number exceeds the limit set by the pressure angle and the addendum. At 20 degrees a rack-cut pinion needs 18 teeth.
